topic.en: What the text is about: how poverty is measured — the basket, the relative line, multidimensional measures and why no correct line exists.
topic.kk: Мәтін не туралы: кедейлікті қалай өлшейді — себет, салыстырмалы шек, көпөлшемді шаралар және дұрыс шектің неге жоқ екені.
topic.ru: О чём текст: как измеряют бедность — корзина, относительная черта, многомерные меры и почему правильной черты не существует.

paragraphs.text: Every government that spends money on poverty has first to say what poverty is, and the saying is harder than the spending. A line has to be drawn somewhere on a scale of income or consumption, everyone below it is counted and everyone above it is not, and the line then acquires a political life of its own: it is quoted in speeches, it decides who receives a payment, and moving it reclassifies millions of people without changing anything in their houses.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The oldest method is to price a basket. A statistician lists what a household needs to avoid deprivation — food providing a stated number of calories, plus an allowance for housing, fuel and clothing — and the cost of that list becomes the line. The method is transparent and it hides a great many judgements: which foods, bought at which shop, cooked with which fuel, for a household of what size and shape. Two competent teams working in the same city can produce baskets that differ by a third.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The alternative is to define poverty relative to the society around it. A common European measure counts households below sixty per cent of the median income, which makes the line move with national prosperity and measures distance from the ordinary rather than distance from survival. It has an awkward property that critics enjoy pointing out: in a recession where all incomes fall together, the median falls too, and measured poverty can decline in a year when everyone has less.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Both approaches share a problem that has nothing to do with lines. Income is a poor description of what a household can actually consume, because it ignores savings, debts, unpaid work, food grown at home and the cost of a disability, and because it is measured for a year while hardship arrives by the week. A household that is above any line in annual terms may be unable to pay for heating in February, and no measure based on an annual figure will see that.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Multidimensional measures were designed to answer this. Instead of one number they count deprivations: a household is asked whether it has electricity, clean water, a school-age child out of school, an adult with less than a stated level of schooling, a floor of earth, and so on, and is counted as poor when it lacks a set number of these. The results often disagree with income measures in useful ways, identifying districts that look adequate on paper and lack every service, and they have a corresponding weakness: the choice of indicators, and of how many are needed, is a judgement that changes the answer.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The international line has its own history. A global figure intended to allow comparison between countries was built by taking the national lines of the poorest countries and converting them into a single currency, and it has been revised upwards several times as prices and data improved. Each revision changes the world total by hundreds of millions of people, which produces headlines about poverty rising or falling that describe a change in the statistic rather than in anyone’s life.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Measurement also has a political economy. A line that is low produces small numbers, which suit a government reporting progress; a line that is high produces large ones, which suit an organisation seeking funds. Statistical offices that are independent of both tend to produce the least convenient figures for everyone, which is a reasonable working test of whether an office is independent. Several countries now publish two or three measures side by side rather than defending a single one.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The honest position is that there is no correct line, and that this does not make measurement pointless. What matters is that a measure is stated openly, applied consistently, and reported alongside the others, so that a fall can be checked against a second and a third. Poverty statistics are not a photograph of hardship; they are an instrument with a known bias, and an instrument of that kind is still worth more than an argument conducted entirely in anecdotes. The question to ask of any figure is therefore not whether it is true but which judgements went into it, and whether the person quoting it knows what they were.
paragraphs.label: H
